analysis.one_liner: Forces agencies to prove major regulations' benefits outweigh costs and lets Congress veto the result.
analysis.headline: The Senate debated the bill through July 1995 but cut off debate three times without reaching the 60 votes needed; the final tally was 58-40, and the bill never came to a final passage vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have overhauled how federal agencies write regulations. Any rule expected to cost the economy $100 million or more would need a formal cost-benefit analysis, a risk assessment, and could be thrown out by a vote of Congress. It would also have suspended legal deadlines requiring agencies to issue rules, made it easier for regulated parties to challenge and void rules in court, and created a petition process to force agencies to redo expensive rules already on the books.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses subject to federal health, safety, environmental, and workplace rules gain the most: every major rule would face a cost-benefit test, a congressional veto point, tougher court review, and new petitions that could force repeal or revision of costly rules. Small businesses gain new rights to challenge agencies' small-business analyses in court.

how_it_helps.text: No major rule could take effect unless the agency found that its benefits justify its costs and that it beats all reasonable alternatives, giving regulated parties a ready-made argument against costly rules.

Any person subject to a major rule could petition the agency, the OMB Director, or the President to perform a cost-benefit analysis, and the agency would have to revoke or amend the rule if the analysis showed costs outweigh benefits.

Courts could set aside rules lacking substantial support in the rulemaking file and had to reject agency interpretations outside the range of permissible readings of the underlying statute, lowering the odds that regulations survive challenge.
Small businesses gain the right to sue over agencies' certifications and analyses under the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

Agencies would have to publish proposed review schedules for existing expensive rules and complete review of them within roughly ten years, with priorities aimed at rules that could be amended or eliminated.

analysis.who_pays: People who rely on federal health, safety, environmental, and workplace protections bear the cost: agencies would have to clear new analytical and procedural hurdles before issuing protections, statutory and court-ordered rulemaking deadlines would be suspended, and Congress could kill any major rule by passing a resolution of disapproval. Delays would also fall on the public waiting for rules the law already requires.

drawbacks.text: All statutory and court-ordered deadlines requiring agencies to issue rules would be suspended for two years, delaying protections already required by law and owed to the public.
A major rule could never take effect if Congress passed a joint resolution of disapproval, putting every expensive rule at the mercy of a legislative vote.
The bill narrows judicial review in ways that make agency interpretations easier to overturn, weakening the legal foundation of health, safety, and environmental rules.

It creates an affirmative defense against civil or criminal penalties for anyone who reasonably concluded from a rule's stated basis that they were in compliance, which regulated parties could invoke after violating a rule.
The bill would have given the President or a designee (including the Vice President) sweeping power to review and police agency rulemaking, with that review itself immune from judicial challenge.

The bill did contain genuine process improvements: minimum 60-day public comment periods, mandatory disclosure of communications about regulatory review, and clearer public risk information, which its supporters could cite honestly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Cost-benefit analysis, peer review, and longer public comment periods have real value, and the bill's public-transparency provisions were legitimate good-government ideas. But the core of the bill was built to make expensive regulation harder: a benefits-justify-costs gate on every major rule, suspended legal deadlines, a congressional veto, narrowed court review, and petitions to reopen existing rules. Those mechanisms would have slowed or stopped health, safety, and environmental protections that ordinary people depend on, while the financial, banking, and communications rulebooks were carved out of the toughest requirements. The transparency gains do not offset the scale of the roadblocks.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate spent three weeks debating the bill but opponents refused to let it come to a final vote, and three attempts to end debate all fell short of the 60 votes needed, so the bill never got an up-or-down vote and died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dole introduced the bill on February 2, 1995, with 30 original cosponsors, all Republicans.
Both the Judiciary and Governmental Affairs Committees reported amended substitutes on May 26, 1995, and the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar.
The Senate took the bill up in late June 1995 and debated it through most of July.
Cloture (the vote needed to end debate and force a final vote, requiring 60 senators) failed three times on the substitute amendment: 48-46 on July 17, 53-47 on July 18, and 58-40 on July 20, 1995.
On the final cloture vote, all 54 Senate Republicans voted yes while 40 of 46 Democrats voted no; the bill never came to a final passage vote.
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, with the bill still on the calendar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on federal health, safety, environmental, and workplace protections came out ahead, because the bill never reached a final vote and never became law. The bill's cosponsors and the industries it would have relieved of costly rules did not get what they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on federal health and safety rules

sides.party_line_note: The fight split almost entirely by party: on the final cloture vote all 54 Republicans voted yes while 40 of 46 Democrats voted no, and only 4 Democrats ever crossed over.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturing, chemicals, energy, and other businesses subject to federal rules)
industries.note: The bill would have forced every major rule through cost-benefit analysis, congressional review, tougher court scrutiny, and petitions to reopen existing rules, cutting compliance costs across the board. Those savings would come at the expense of delayed or weaker health, safety, and environmental protections.

The reported bill excluded rules on bank safety and soundness, Federal Reserve monetary policy, the Federal Home Loan Banks, credit unions, and Federal Election Commission and certain Federal Communications Commission rules from the 'major rule' definition, so the new cost-benefit hurdles would not touch their regulators' work even as other industries faced them.

Small entities would gain new rights to sue over agencies' small-business analyses and certifications, and each major-rule analysis would have to assess effects on businesses with fewer than 100 employees.
